title: Greedy Best-First in Lisbon: Fast but Can Fail ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First slice through Lisbon’s streets by always choosing the node that looks closest to the goal. Then see where it can get trapped—faster than A*, but not always the best route.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison—why it rushes toward the goal ⚡ but sometimes fails. 
In this Lisbon (Alfama) map run, Greedy Best-First expands the frontier node with the smallest heuristic h(n) (typically straight-line distance). It ignores actual path cost so it may chase “getting closer” while stepping into a dead-end or a long detour.

Mechanics (quick, real):
• Evaluation: f(n)=h(n)
• Uses a priority queue ordered by h(n)
• Can be dangerously overconfident when the heuristic doesn’t reflect obstacles/travel constraints

Takeaway: Greedy is great for speed when h(n) correlates with true distance—but when the environment lies to your heuristic, A*’s g(n)+h(n) tends to recover.

Debate: In your experience, when is “fast enough” worth risking a wrong turn—greedy heuristics, or always pay the A* cost?

In this real-city (Lisbon • Alfama) pathfinding visualization, we compare how Greedy Best-First picks the next node using only the heuristic h(n), while A* typically balances path cost g(n) with h(n).

You’ll see: 
1) The greedy priority-queue expansion behavior

3) The key difference that makes A* more reliable for optimal routes
